paragraphs.title: The Wicked and the Sense That God Is Distant

answers: Why the LORD stands afar off
easy.explanation: Psalm 10:1 asks, “Why standest thou afar off, O LORD?”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask at the beginning of the passage?

easy.explanation: Verse 2 says, “The wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor.”
Verse 4 says that the wicked “will not seek after God.”
easy.q: What does the wicked person refuse to do?

answers: He believes that God is not involved in his thoughts or actions
He trusts that the poor will protect him
medium.explanation: The wicked person does not seek God and acts as though God is absent from his thoughts.
medium.q: Why does the wicked person feel secure in his wrongdoing?

medium.explanation: “Devices” refers to the wicked plans or schemes they have imagined.
medium.q: What does “devices” mean in the phrase “the devices that they have imagined”?

answers: As someone who rules over the wicked
As someone who is pursued and oppressed
As someone who is hiding from God
medium.explanation: The poor are described as being persecuted by the proud wicked.
medium.q: How is the poor person portrayed in this passage?

answers: The wicked prosper while the poor suffer
The poor rule while the wicked serve
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts the wicked person’s pride and success with the poor person’s distress.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in these verses?

answers: He believes the wicked are right
He feels that God’s presence is hidden during trouble
He does not notice the suffering of the poor
challenge.explanation: The question about God standing afar off and hiding Himself expresses a sense of divine distance.
challenge.q: What does the opening question reveal about the psalmist’s experience?

answers: As a defender of the weak
As a proud persecutor who devises evil
challenge.explanation: The wicked person is proud, persecutes the poor, and imagines harmful devices.
challenge.q: How is the wicked person characterized morally?

paragraphs.title: The Ways of the Wicked and Their Harm to the Weak

easy.explanation: Verse 7 says, “His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud.”
easy.q: What is the mouth of the wicked full of?

answers: In the lurking places of the villages
easy.explanation: Verse 8 says, “He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages.”
easy.q: Where does the wicked person sit?

easy.explanation: The passage repeatedly describes the wicked person lying in wait to catch the poor.
easy.q: Whom does the wicked person seek to catch?

answers: He believes he will never be moved or suffer adversity
He depends on the help of the poor
medium.explanation: He says in his heart, “I shall not be moved: for I shall never be in adversity.”
medium.q: What makes the wicked person feel confident?

answers: Public places where everyone can see him
Hidden places from which he can ambush others
medium.explanation: The phrase describes concealed places where the wicked waits to attack.
medium.q: What does “lurking places” mean in this context?

answers: They keep him from harming anyone
They are part of the methods he uses to trap the vulnerable
They cause him to defend the poor
medium.explanation: His deceptive speech accompanies his secret ambushes and traps.
medium.q: How do deceit and fraud contribute to the wicked person’s actions?

answers: He hides and waits to seize the poor
challenge.explanation: Like a lion in its den, he secretly waits to catch the poor.
challenge.q: Why is the image of a lion appropriate to the wicked person?

answers: The wicked person’s attacks are deliberate and planned
The wicked person does not know what he is doing
The poor are actually the pursuers
challenge.explanation: The repeated ambush imagery shows careful planning rather than accidental harm.
challenge.q: What does the repeated imagery of hiding, waiting, and nets suggest?

answers: He says he will fall, but he stands firm
He claims he cannot be moved, yet he acts secretly and fearfully
He says he is poor, yet he helps the poor
challenge.explanation: Although he boasts of security, he relies on hiding, crouching, and secret attacks.
challenge.q: What contradiction appears between the wicked person’s words and his behavior?

paragraphs.title: The Psalmist's Plea for Intervention and Judgment

easy.explanation: The prayer begins, “Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up thine hand.”
easy.q: To whom does the psalmist cry for help?
Whom does the psalmist ask God not to forget?

easy.explanation: Verse 15 says, “Break thou the arm of the wicked and the evil man.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to break?

answers: To reveal His power and act against injustice
To hide the suffering of the poor
medium.explanation: The request is for God to intervene powerfully on behalf of the oppressed.
medium.q: Why does the psalmist ask God to arise and lift up His hand?

answers: You will not call the wicked to account
medium.explanation: The wicked person assumes that God will not demand an accounting for his actions.
medium.q: What does “thou wilt not require it” mean in the context?

answers: Only the prosperity of the wicked
medium.explanation: Verse 14 says, “thou beholdest mischief and spite.”
medium.q: What does the psalmist affirm that God sees?

answers: The passage moves from describing wickedness to asking God for judgment
The passage moves from praising the wicked to ignoring the poor
The passage moves from prayer to celebrating oppression
challenge.explanation: The psalmist responds to the wicked person’s claims by pleading for divine intervention.
challenge.q: What major movement occurs in these verses?

answers: It agrees that God has forgotten
It declares that God sees mischief and spite
It avoids discussing the wicked person
challenge.explanation: The psalmist explicitly says that God beholds injustice and can requite it.
challenge.q: How does the prayer answer the wicked person’s claim that God does not see?

answers: Removing the wicked person’s power to harm
challenge.explanation: The arm represents strength and power, so breaking it symbolizes defeating the oppressor.
challenge.q: What does breaking the arm of the wicked symbolize?

paragraphs.title: God's Kingship and Protection of the Humble

easy.explanation: Verse 16 declares, “The LORD is King for ever and ever.”
easy.q: Who is King for ever and ever?

easy.explanation: Verse 17 says, “LORD, thou hast heard the desire of the humble.”
easy.q: Whose desire does the LORD hear?

easy.explanation: Verse 18 says that God judges “the fatherless and the oppressed.”

answers: His kingship includes hearing and judging on behalf of the oppressed
His kingship causes Him to ignore the weak
His kingship strengthens the wicked against the poor
medium.explanation: God’s rule is shown through His attention to the humble and His judgment for the oppressed.
medium.q: How is God’s kingship connected with His care for the weak?

medium.explanation: The oppressed are those who suffer under unjust or harsh treatment.
medium.q: What does “oppressed” mean in this passage?

answers: The wicked will oppress more people
The weak will no longer be oppressed by earthly people
The humble will remain silent forever
medium.explanation: The final verse says that the man of the earth may no more oppress.
medium.q: What is the desired result of God’s judgment?

answers: It confirms that God never acts
It presents God as the eternal King who hears and judges
It returns attention to the success of the wicked
challenge.explanation: The conclusion shows God actively hearing the humble and judging for the oppressed.
challenge.q: How does the ending answer the feeling of distance expressed at the beginning?

answers: God provides an ongoing response to the needs of the weak
The weak are responsible for the oppression
challenge.explanation: The sequence portrays God as attentive, strengthening, and acting in justice.
challenge.q: What is suggested by the sequence of hearing, preparing, and judging?

answers: The earthly man oppresses, while God judges to protect the weak
The earthly man listens, while God oppresses
The earthly man is the eternal King, while God hides
challenge.explanation: The verse contrasts human oppression with God’s just defense of the fatherless and oppressed.
challenge.q: What final contrast is made between the oppressor and God?
